title: What is the difference between static variables and instance variables in Java?
shortTitle: Difference between static variables and instance variables

s1_definition.profdef: A static variable, also called a class variable, belongs to the class and exists as a single shared copy regardless of how many objects are created; it is initialized when the class is loaded and lives in the method area or Metaspace. An instance variable belongs to each object and exists as a separate copy per instance; it is initialized when the object is constructed and lives on the heap inside that object. Changing a static variable is visible to all instances, whereas changing an instance variable affects only that one object.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, a static variable is like the bank's single policy interest rate displayed at head office; there is exactly one of it and every account sees the same value. An instance variable is like each customer's own account balance; Rajesh has his own balance and Priya has hers, and changing Rajesh's balance does not touch Priya's. The shared head-office rate is static; the personal balances are instance variables, one per account object.
s1_definition.oneliner: Static variables are one shared copy per class; instance variables are a separate copy per object.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A static variable, also called a class variable, belongs to the class and exists as a single shared copy regardless of how many objects are created; it is initialized when the class is loaded and lives in the method area or Metaspace. An instance variable belongs to each object and exists as a separate copy per instance; it is initialized when the object is constructed and lives on the heap inside that object. Changing a static variable is visible to all instances, whereas changing an instance variable affects only that one object.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, a static variable is like the bank's single policy interest rate displayed at head office; there is exactly one of it and every account sees the same value. An instance variable is like each customer's own account balance; Rajesh has his own balance and Priya has hers, and changing Rajesh's balance does not touch Priya's. The shared head-office rate is static; the personal balances are instance variables, one per account object.

**One line to remember:** Static variables are one shared copy per class; instance variables are a separate copy per object.

sections.s2_technical:
An instance variable is declared inside a class without the static keyword. Every time you create an object, a fresh set of instance variables is allocated for that object. Rajesh's Account object and Priya's Account object each have their own `balance` field. Modifying one does not affect the other because they are physically separate storage on the heap. Instance variables get their default values, such as 0 or null, when the object is created, and are typically set in the constructor.

A static variable is declared with the static keyword. There is exactly one copy for the entire class, shared by all instances and also accessible without any instance through the class name. It is initialized when the class is loaded, which happens once. A static variable is the right tool for data that is logically shared, like a system-wide transfer counter, a configuration constant, or a cache shared across all objects of the type.

Access differs too. An instance variable requires an object reference, like `rajesh.getBalance()`. A static variable should be accessed through the class name, like `TransferService.getTotalTransfers()`, although Java also allows accessing it via an instance, which is discouraged because it hides the fact that it is shared.

Lifecycle differs. Instance variables live as long as their object is reachable and are garbage collected with the object. Static variables live as long as the class is loaded, which is usually the lifetime of the application, so they can unintentionally keep memory alive. A senior nuance is thread-safety: because static variables are shared, concurrent writes from multiple threads create race conditions unless you synchronize or use atomic types. Instance variables are safer when each thread works on its own object, but shared instances still need care. Another nuance is memory: a static collection that grows without bound is a classic memory leak, because it is never collected while the class is loaded, which in a long-running banking server can slowly exhaust the heap.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank needs each account to carry its own balance, independent of every other account. This is exactly what an instance variable provides — one copy per object.

Problem 2 — The bank also needs a single system-wide count of how many accounts have been opened, shared across all account objects. This is exactly what a static variable provides — one shared copy per class.

Problem 3 — The team must show that changing Rajesh's balance never affects Priya's, while opening any new account increments the same shared counter. This is exactly the difference between per-object and per-class state.

The code has an `Account` class with an instance balance field and a static accounts-opened counter incremented in the constructor, and a `StaticVsInstanceDemo` main class that creates Rajesh and Priya and mutates balances independently.
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile
javac -d out src/main/java/com/bank/state/StaticVsInstanceDemo.java

# Run
java -cp out com.bank.state.StaticVsInstanceDemo
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three accounts created, Rajesh SAV2001 at 1,000,000, Priya CUR3001 at 250,000, and later Amit SAV2002 at 5,000, with a 50000 debit on Rajesh.

Step 1: Rajesh's Account object is created. His instance balance is set to 1,000,000, and the shared static accountsOpened counter goes from 0 to 1.

Step 2: Priya's Account object is created. She gets her own instance balance of 250,000, completely separate from Rajesh's, and the shared counter goes from 1 to 2.

Step 3: The static counter is read through the class name and reports 2, because it is a single shared value seen by all.

Step 4: Rajesh is debited 50,000. Only his instance balance changes, from 1,000,000 to 950,000. Priya's instance balance remains 250,000, proving instance variables are per-object.

Step 5: A third account for Amit is created. His own instance balance is 5,000, and the shared counter goes from 2 to 3.

Step 6: The static counter now reports 3, visible regardless of which object you ask through, confirming that static state is one shared copy while instance balances stayed independent.

```text
INFO: Accounts opened so far = 2
INFO: Rajesh balance = 950000.00
INFO: Priya  balance = 250000.00
INFO: Accounts opened so far = 3
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Account.accountsOpened (static)  ── ONE shared box ──┐
                                                       │
  new Account(SAV2001) → instance balance=1,000,000 ──┼→ counter 0→1
  new Account(CUR3001) → instance balance=  250,000 ──┼→ counter 1→2
                                                       │
  rajesh.debit(50000)  → SAV2001 balance 1,000,000→950,000
                         CUR3001 balance 250,000 (UNCHANGED)
                                                       │
  new Account(SAV2002) → instance balance=    5,000 ──┴→ counter 2→3

  Instance vars: 3 separate boxes (one per object)
  Static var   : 1 shared box (counter = 3)
```

```text
   lives in      Metaspace             heap (inside object)

   thread-safety shared → needs sync    per-object → safer
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The difference between static variables and instance variables comes down to who owns the data and how many copies exist. A static variable, also called a class variable, belongs to the class and exists as a single shared copy no matter how many objects I create. It is initialized when the class is loaded and lives in the method area or Metaspace. An instance variable belongs to each object and exists as a separate copy per instance, allocated on the heap inside that object and initialized when the object is constructed.

The practical consequence is visibility. If I change a static variable, every instance sees the change because they all share the one copy. If I change an instance variable, only that one object is affected. In our account model, each account carries its own balance as an instance variable, so debiting Rajesh's account never touches Priya's. But the system-wide count of accounts opened is a static variable, so every time any account object is constructed, that one shared counter goes up, and reading it gives the same value no matter which object I ask through.

Access and lifecycle also differ. Instance variables are accessed through an object reference and are garbage collected along with their object. Static variables should be accessed through the class name and live as long as the class is loaded, which is usually the whole application lifetime.

The senior points I always raise are about safety. Because static variables are shared, concurrent writes from multiple threads cause race conditions unless I synchronize or use atomic types, which is a real concern in a multi-threaded banking server. And a static collection that grows without bound is a classic memory leak, since it is never collected while the class is loaded. So my rule is to use instance variables for per-entity state like balances, use static variables only for genuinely shared data, and keep that shared static state either immutable or carefully synchronized.
